item.title: When Scatter Plots Hide the Data: Diagnosing Ties and Choosing the Right Display in R
item.description: arXiv:2610.36590v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scatter plots draw one mark per observation, so observations that share a location are hidden. In a two-item Likert survey of 2,757 respondents, 98.7% of the data lie under other points and the plot shows only 36 dots. The density-distribution sunflower plot of Dupont and Plummer addresses this by drawing raw points in sparse regions and sunflowers, whose petals count observations, in dense ones. It is not available in R, and its single petal weight for dense cells fails when cell counts span more than an order of magnitude: small dense cells collapse to one petal, and the count a reader decodes can be wrong by 150% or more. We propose geometric petal tiers, in which each cell uses the smallest weight among 1, b, b2, . . . observations per petal that keeps its flower within P petals. Every flower then has between about P/b and P petals, and the relative error of every decoded count is below b/(2P), 17.9% at the defaults b = 5 and P = 14. We also define tie diagnostics and decision rules that use them to choose between an ordinary scatter plot, jitter or transparency, a classic sunflower plot and geometric tiers. Both are implemented in the ggplot2 extension ggsunflower. We illustrate the methods on survey, automotive, historical and large commercial data, and in a simulation over 35 conditions geometric tiers keep the worst-cell error at or below 14% where a single weight reaches a median of 251%.
item.dc:creator: Sameera Viswakula

item.title: Bayesian Treed Vecchia Gaussian Process Emulation via Sequential Monte Carlo
item.description: arXiv:2610.36770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer models (or simulators) are used in many scientific domains to understand and predict real-world processes, but they are expensive to run. One way to address this hurdle is to use Gaussian processes (GPs). For complex physical systems such as storm surge, simulator outputs often exhibit heterogeneous structures, and many nonstationary GP methods become impractical with several inputs and tens of thousands of runs. To address these issues, we combine the divide-and-conquer idea of treed GP models with Vecchia approximations in a Bayesian treed Vecchia GP (TVGP) model. The model uses the Bayesian classification and regression tree prior for random recursive partitioning of the input domain. Within each leaf, a Vecchia approximation allows efficient likelihood evaluation. For Bayesian inference, we develop a sequential Monte Carlo algorithm that explores tree space as an alternative to reversible-jump Markov chain Monte Carlo. The method is demonstrated on synthetic examples with two and ten inputs and on a storm-surge simulator with seven inputs and up to 50,649 training runs. TVGP has the smallest prediction error in both synthetic examples and with the larger storm-surge training set, although its predictive intervals undercover in the example with ten inputs and the storm-surge application.
item.dc:creator: Cong Ye, Pulong Ma

item.title: Reducing Complexity of Pseudo-Marginal Sequential Monte Carlo via Hierarchical Tempering
item.description: arXiv:2610.37082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Bayesian approach to inverse problems provides a powerful framework for inferring unknown parameters from noisy observations. Among the computationally most challenging statistical inference problems are problems with intractable likelihoods, especially if no unbiased likelihood estimator is available. We focus on a class of such problems, where a biased likelihood estimator is obtained through a stochastic approximation of a forward map (stochastic solver). Obtaining an empirical posterior approximation in applications is very expensive due to the repeated stochastic solver evaluations required by standard sampling methods. To address this computational bottleneck, we develop a novel algorithm based on a density-tempered marginalized Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampler. Our approach (hierarchical SMC) accelerates inference by leveraging a hierarchy of stochastic solvers with increasing accuracy both along the tempering sequence and within mutation stages of the SMC sampler. We establish, under additional assumptions, that the asymptotic speedup is proportional to the number of tempering stages $T$. We demonstrate computational gains on several examples, including a nonlinear, high-contrast inverse problem arising in photoacoustic medical imaging. On this problem, we demonstrate a speedup by a factor of 14.3, reducing the inference wall-clock time from about 4.6 days to 7.7 hours on an NVIDIA A40 GPU.
item.dc:creator: Josef Mart\'inek, Julian Hofstadler, Alexander M. G. Cox, Robert Scheichl

item.title: Mirror Likelihood for Modeling Manifold Data with Application on Correlation Time Series
item.description: arXiv:2610.36448v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Manifold-valued data arise in a wide range of scientific applications. Existing statistical methods typically follow either an intrinsic approach, which characterizes the manifold itself via quantities such as geodesic distance or the Fr\'echet mean, or an extrinsic approach, which embeds the manifold into an ambient Euclidean space, performs unconstrained statistical estimation, and projects the result back to the manifold. While the latter is conceptually and computationally simple, likelihood-based extrinsic solutions remain scarce, due to the lack of a general recipe for choosing an embedding map and for characterizing its impact on the transformed distribution. In this article, we tackle the problem using an augmented likelihood approach: we view the manifold-valued data as the Fenchel mirror map of a latent variable, which is nearly unconstrained, and model the latent variable with a canonical distribution, such as Gaussian. The key transform, the Fenchel mirror map, is a generalization of the Euclidean projection and can effectively map into the interior of the manifold. Taking a Bayesian approach, the proposed framework enjoys a generative model interpretation and an augmented likelihood free from intractable normalization constants, and it supports principled uncertainty quantification and flexible model-based extensions. We study the theoretical and computational properties of the framework and demonstrate its utility in analyzing neuroimaging data of high-dimensional correlation time series, where each correlation matrix is rank deficient.
item.dc:creator: Luis Hasenauer, Arkaprava Roy, Leo Duan

item.title: Coupled unbiased MCMC for estimating Shapley effects under dependent inputs
item.description: arXiv:2610.36690v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In global sensitivity analysis, Shapley effects provide a game-theoretic allocation of output variance among potentially dependent inputs. Their computation typically requires repeated conditional sampling, which can be challenging even when independent samples from the joint input distribution can be generated exactly. This difficulty arises naturally in hierarchical models, where conditioning on arbitrary subsets need not follow the generative order. To efficiently estimate Shapley effects under such dependence between input variables, we propose a permutation-based framework using coupled unbiased Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). Our proposed method combines two complementary coupling mechanisms: (i) a joint coupling of conditional distributions along a random permutation, designed to reduce the variance of estimated marginal contributions, and (ii) a meeting-based coupling of Markov chains that removes finite-time MCMC bias through a telescoping correction. Under suitable conditions, we prove that the resulting estimators for the unnormalized Shapley effects are unbiased, and have finite variance and finite expected computational cost. Numerical experiments with various test cases illustrate the computational efficiency of the proposed method.
item.dc:creator: Masataka Hirono, Takashi Goda

item.title: Efficient Bootstrap Calibration of Generalized Posteriors with Importance Reweighting
item.description: arXiv:2610.37232v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The learning rate of a generalized posterior governs posterior uncertainty but typically has no canonical value. Generalized posterior calibration (GPC) selects this rate by matching bootstrap-estimated credible-interval coverage to its nominal level, often requiring repeated posterior simulation. We propose GPC via importance reweighting (GPC-IRW), which reuses draws from a reference posterior fitted to the original data across bootstrap resamples and candidate learning rates. For quantile-based intervals of a scalar functional, we express the coverage criterion in terms of bootstrap posterior cumulative distribution functions, avoiding computation of individual bootstrap credible intervals. Safeguards based on importance-weight effective sample size and proximity to coverage-decision boundaries invoke reweighting from cached bootstrap-specific draws or direct posterior simulation when necessary. Under the stated regularity conditions, with numerical error tending to zero, we show that median-centered calibration preserves the first-order learning-rate target and achieves asymptotically nominal coverage. The approach extends to independent clusters through cluster-level resampling. Simulations yield coverage and interval lengths comparable to those of existing GPC algorithms at substantially lower computational cost. In an exoplanet mass-radius analysis, GPC-IRW achieves 6.7- and 9.6-fold speedups over MCMC-based calibration in the single-planet and full-sample analyses, respectively, while illustrating the effects of within-host dependence.
item.dc:creator: Masahiro Tanaka

item.title: Unifying Sparse Estimation of Precision and Covariance Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2403.12357v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Penalized maximum likelihood is a widely used approach to estimate a sparse precision or a sparse covariance matrix. A zero in the precision matrix encodes a conditional independence and a zero in the covariance matrix a marginal independence, and the two estimators have been developed separately, each with its own algorithm. We show that these two problems can be unified via a single reparametrization of the last column of either matrix. This reparametrization decouples the likelihood function for each problem to a one-dimensional minimization followed by a penalized multiple regression. Our approach applies to any penalty that is separable in the off-diagonal entries and linear on the diagonal. When the penalty is the $\ell_1$ norm, it unifies the graphical Lasso and the covariance graphical Lasso algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Aramayis Dallakyan, Mohsen Pourahmadi

item.title: ProjGuard: Safety Monitoring for Computer-Use Agents via Low-Dimensional Projections
item.description: arXiv:2605.13631v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Computer-use agents are increasingly capable of operating on real operating systems, but this capability has also increased their exposure to prompt injection and other adversarial content that can manipulate their behavior during interaction. Existing defenses typically rely on analyzing the prompt or each potentially malicious input with a second large model at inference time, which can limit coverage or increase deployment cost. We propose ProjGuard, a lightweight runtime monitor that derives a scalar risk signal from the agent's accumulated response history using a supervised linear projection. The monitor evaluates this signal at each step and raises an alert when it exceeds a fitted threshold. When an alert is raised, we selectively activate an auxiliary vision-language model (VLM) to propose the next action and steer execution back toward task completion. Experiments on OS-Harm show that monitoring with on-demand VLM intervention reduces the unsafe rate from 16% to 3% while improving task completion from 59% to 65%. We further evaluate transfer to RiosWorld, where the method remains competitive, reaching 4% unsafe and 64% completion. Overall, these results support a hierarchical safety strategy that combines continuous response monitoring with selective multimodal intervention.
item.dc:creator: Kebin Contreras, Carlos Hinojosa, Jorge Bacca, Bernard Ghanem

item.title: StablePCA: Distributionally Robust Learning of Shared Representations from Multi-Source Data
item.description: arXiv:2505.00940v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When synthesizing multi-source high-dimensional data, a key objective is to extract low-dimensional representations that effectively approximate the original features across different sources. Such representations facilitate the discovery of transferable structures and help mitigate systematic biases such as batch effects. We introduce Stable Principal Component Analysis (StablePCA), a distributionally robust framework for constructing stable latent representations by maximizing the worst-case explained variance over multiple sources. A primary challenge in extending classical PCA to the multi-source setting lies in the nonconvex rank constraint, which renders the StablePCA formulation a nonconvex optimization problem. To overcome this challenge, we conduct a convex relaxation of StablePCA and develop an efficient Mirror-Prox algorithm to solve the relaxed problem, with global convergence guarantees. Since the relaxed problem generally differs from the original formulation, we further introduce a data-dependent certificate to assess how well the algorithm solves the original nonconvex problem and establish the condition under which the relaxation is tight. Finally, we explore alternative distributionally robust formulations of multi-source PCA based on different loss functions.
item.dc:creator: Zhenyu Wang, Molei Liu, Jing Lei, Francis Bach, Zijian Guo

item.title: Two-sample comparison through additive tree models for density ratios
item.description: arXiv:2508.03059v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The ratio of two densities provides a direct characterization of their differences. We consider the two-sample comparison problem by estimating this ratio given i.i.d. observations from two distributions. To this end, we propose additive tree models for density ratio estimation along with efficient algorithms using a new loss function, the balancing loss. The loss allows tree-based models to be trained using several algorithms originally designed for supervised learning, such as forward-stagewise optimization and gradient boosting. Moreover, the balancing loss resembles an exponential family kernel, and it can serve as a pseudo-likelihood with conjugate priors. This property enables generalized Bayesian inference on the density ratio using backfitting samplers designed for Bayesian additive regression trees (BART). Our Bayesian strategy provides uncertainty quantification for the inferred density ratio, which is critical for applications involving high-dimensional and data-limited distributions with potentially substantial uncertainty. We further show connections of the balancing loss to the exponential loss in binary classification and to the variational form of f-divergence, particularly the squared Hellinger distance. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed boosting algorithms achieve high accuracy at low computational cost, and that the Bayesian additive tree is competitive in accuracy while additionally providing uncertainty quantification, which the compared estimators do not offer. Finally, we demonstrate its application to assessing the quality of generative models for microbiome compositional data.
item.dc:creator: Naoki Awaya, Yuliang Xu, Li Ma
